analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1992 law that re-regulated cable TV rates, ending federal price caps on cable service.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 1992 cable rate rules drew 12 cosponsors, all Republicans, but never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed most of the 1992 Cable Television Consumer Protection and Competition Act, the law that put federal price regulation back on the cable industry after years of steep rate increases, keeping only the rules that let broadcast stations negotiate payment from cable systems. It would also have wiped out the Federal Communications Commission's rules carrying out the 1992 law. The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable television operators. The bill would strike down the 1992 Cable Act's rate regulations, letting cable companies set their own prices again, and would void the FCC rules that put those price caps into practice. Broadcast stations would also keep the retransmission-consent right to charge cable systems for carrying their signals, which the bill specifically preserved.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable TV operators freed from rate caps

how_it_helps.text: It would have restored cable operators' freedom to set their own rates by repealing the 1992 law's price regulations and applying the Communications Act as if the 1992 amendments had never been made.
It would have voided, on the day of enactment, any FCC regulations written to implement the 1992 law, removing rate caps in practice immediately rather than waiting for a phase-out.
It would have preserved broadcasters' retransmission-consent rights under section 6 of the 1992 law, the one piece of the 1992 Act the bill left standing.

analysis.who_pays: Cable subscribers would pay. The 1992 law let the FCC cap and roll back cable rates; repealing it would remove that price protection, and the FCC rules written to enforce it would stop being effective the day the bill was enacted.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 1992 law would have removed the FCC's rate caps and rollback authority, leaving cable subscribers without federal price protection in markets where cable systems faced little or no competition.
Repeal would also have swept away the 1992 law's other consumer provisions along with the rate rules, since the bill applied the amended Communications Act as if the 1992 Act had never been enacted.

Supporters of repeal argued that rate regulation discourages investment in cable systems and that competition, not price caps, should discipline pricing; the bill offered no substitute mechanism to guarantee that competition would actually materialize.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For cable subscribers, the costs outweighed the benefits. The bill's entire practical effect was to strip away federal price regulation on cable service and void the FCC rules enforcing it, with nothing replacing the protection except the hope that competition would hold prices down. Its one surviving benefit, keeping retransmission-consent rules, mainly served broadcasters. The bill's death without a vote meant subscribers kept the 1992 law's rate protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then a subcommittee and never got a vote, dying when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill would have repealed the Cable Television Consumer Protection and Competition Act of 1992, except for its retransmission-consent provisions, and restored the Communications Act as if the 1992 law had never been enacted.
It would have made FCC regulations issued to implement the 1992 law ineffective upon enactment, wiping out the rate rules in practice as well as in statute.

The bill was introduced on October 12, 1993, referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, then sent to its Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, where it stayed with no further action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill drew 12 cosponsors, all Republicans, and died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable subscribers came out ahead: the 1992 rate regulations and the FCC's implementing rules stayed in force for the rest of the 103rd Congress. Cable operators, which stood to regain pricing freedom under the bill, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable subscribers kept their rate protections

for.name: Rep. Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 1992 Cable Act on October 12, 1993.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance and never scheduled it for a subcommittee or full-committee vote; it sat there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so positions were never tested on the floor; all 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill died without action in a committee led by Democrats.

industries.note: Repeal would lift the FCC rate regulation imposed by the 1992 law, restoring the industry's freedom to set prices after a period when the FCC was rolling rates back. The industry's gain would come directly out of subscribers' monthly bills.

The bill deliberately preserved the 1992 law's retransmission-consent provisions, which let broadcast stations demand cash payment from cable systems for carrying their signals. That preserves broadcasters' leverage, though the costs of those negotiations tend to flow through to cable subscribers.
